dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: North Steps and Canal Walk have four library windows to share. This route machine runs a small practice schedule with the rule and request counts you give it. A draft claims the desk heard every request. Walk beyond the desk and bring both slips back.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The desk sheet recorded twelve and five. The walking round brings three and eleven more after repeated request numbers are set aside. Keep one rule in the machine while you swap the input. At the weir, you held one setting steady to see what the repair changed.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: You held the rule steady. It ran with seventeen requests from the desk and thirty-one when the walking slips joined it. Both numbers belong to the way they were collected. Now hold the joined tally steady and change the rule to see who gets the windows.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The same joined tally can give different windows to the two districts. The machine follows the rule you give it. Take your two results to Lin so the public notice carries the rule as well as the numbers.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The desk opens during the workday. The walking crew speaks to people as it goes. Bring both collection slips to Ade. Try one rule first on the desk record and then on the joined record. Next, try a second rule on the joined record.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The joined tally reads fifteen for North Steps and sixteen for Canal Walk. A starting window at each keeps both places on the first schedule. A queue rule follows the larger count. An equal split gives both the same number. Put a rule you tested on the public notice.

options.text: Send all four windows to the larger recorded queue.
Leave one starting window in each district, then give the larger count the other two.
Give each district two windows.
Leave the route open for now.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The printed rule and count are beside the desk. A reader left a reply on the Canal Walk rail. They needed something the count could not show.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: One request number tells us a request was made. The reader at Canal Walk has to find a stop at a time they can reach. The window counts leave that question open. Keep the first rule in view and give the next request round a place and a time to check.

options.text: Leave an evening request stop with a time-and-place line.
Give the walking crew a place-and-time line for its next round.
Leave the notice ready.
I kept a separate waiting tally at the Nexus bench.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: At the Nexus, the tray recorded a loan move. Your waiting tally kept a different count. Here the route ledger records requests. A person waiting for an evening window still needs a way to leave that detail. Keep both kinds of record where readers can check them.

options.text: Leave an evening request stop with a time-and-place line.
Give the walking crew a place-and-time line for its next round.
Leave the notice ready.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: Lin sends a place-and-time card to Canal Walk for an evening round. The first four window counts stay on their own dated line by the public desk. A reader finishing work later can tell the crew where and when to meet before the next schedule is drawn.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The walking crew carries a second sheet past the canal stairs. People can give a reachable place and time during the next round. The four window counts remain on the wall while the crew gathers the new details.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: A reader at the low bench can find both district names. The rule, counts and open schedule details run together on the small card. Shall we leave them their own lines?

options.text: Leave a wider route notice at the low bench.
Keep the notice where it is.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The wider sheet gives the trial rule, each district’s count and the next place-and-time check their own lines. A reader can go back to the line they need.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The wider sheet leaves room for the next evening or walking record. Someone at the bench can follow how the first four windows were shared and where to leave a reply.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The plan sends all four windows to Canal Walk, which has sixteen recorded requests. North Steps has fifteen and gets zero in this trial. Lin leaves that count and the zero together on the door. A reader has room to add a question below.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: One window goes to North Steps, three to Canal Walk. The first window lets each district begin on the plan. The extra two follow the larger recorded count. Lin leaves room for a question about when they will happen.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: Both districts get two. The notice puts the equal split alongside the two different counts so a reader can see the rule did the sharing. Lin leaves a clip under the notice for the next reader.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: Three sealed load slips are clipped to the red tray. Each slip gives one courier’s practice arrival. This desk can take one load at each numbered mark.

options.text: Unclip the three slips and place their loads.
Leave the clips in place.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: Three sealed load slips are clipped to the blue tray. Each slip gives one courier’s practice arrival. This desk can take one load at each numbered mark.

options.text: Unclip the three slips and place their loads.
Leave the clips in place.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: Two loads land on the first mark. Leave one beside the desk to wait. The fourth mark takes the last load. Two marks remain empty. The cart has three loads and four places in the shift, but one place is needed twice.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The first, second and fourth marks each take one load. The third stays empty. All three couriers clear the desk as they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The two trays show different outcomes. This rack holds every ordered arrival for three named couriers. Each courier gets the same four slips to draw from, and you put the slip back before the next draw.

options.text: Start filling the rack with rows that keep all three loads apart.
Leave the rack empty.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The first courier gets four choices. Slide their used mark out of the row. Three choices remain for the second courier and two for the third. With the marks all back in play, each of the three can choose any of the four.

options.text: Group the remaining rows where two or more loads share a mark.
Leave the rows ready.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The shared-mark rows fill more than half the rack. If every ordered row has the same chance, exactly five out of eight have a match. This counts matching arrivals in the model. The crew’s bell slip can tell us whether their shifts let the arrivals spread evenly.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The two trays tested what this desk does to known arrivals. The rack counts matches when the marks are equally likely and each draw is independent. The bell slip ties real couriers to the same release. Try a receiving arrangement for one practice shift.

options.text: Ask a helper to take a second load beside the busy mark.
Give the three couriers separate marks and keep one spare.
Leave the arrangement open for now.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: A helper takes a spare crate bracket to Canal Walk. If three loads reach that mark together, someone still has to wait. The first practice tray stays in the hall to compare.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The North Steps clerk pins three separate marks to the practice stand. The counts guarantee room if the assigned marks hold. A spare mark gives someone with a changed shift a place to try.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: Here is the separate convention that the earlier article led you to. Use the folio to keep that promise to find a record apart from the date written on the record you found.

options.text: Line up 30 September and 26 October under their own headings.
Leave the second date in its case.

dialogue.speaker: civic-operator
dialogue.text: The treaty is dated 30 September 1809. The Vincennes convention is dated 26 October. It records a declaration by its listed Wea representatives. The words on the page tell us what the record says. They leave open what happened in the negotiations and how freely people could act.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: An old cabinet card says “Shawnee government.” Fit the folio over the name on the public constitution. Leave the treaty dates in their own slot.

options.text: Expose the full name and the article on its own government.
Leave the cabinet card in place for now.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: This cover names the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. Its constitution sets out its own branches of government. The Absentee Shawnee Tribe and the Shawnee Tribe are separate governments. This copy gives the history shelves a present-day voice with its own name.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: The learner who carried the cabinet card to our desk thought signing a request meant the signer could decide for the street. We use one line for the person who logged a request and another for the body that decides it. Help the next reader see the difference. Keep the real records with their names and dates.

options.text: Hold the two dated treaty records open at North Steps.
Clip the full constitutional name and source directions beside the Canal Walk practice ledger.
Leave the new lines at my desk.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: A desk reader goes back to Article 5 and then to the October convention. They ask for each date the next time a deed is copied. The constitutional record stays at its own stand.

dialogue.speaker: civic-clerk
dialogue.text: A Canal reader follows the named constitution back to its own case. They mark the difference between a request and a decision on the practice ledger. The two treaty records stay together at Dispatch.

missions.title: A Place on the Route
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How do the people we count and the rules we use shape the service others can reach?
missions.stake: If the dispatch rule stays as it is, one street never gets the mobile library.

objectives.title: Cross into the Civic Machine district and meet Ade.
Find the desk and walking-crew request slips.

objectives.title: Try the same rule on both request tallies and check the desk heading.

kq.action: hold the allocation rule fixed and change the request sample

objectives.title: Try two different rules with the joined request tally.
Choose a tested rule and put the four windows on Lin’s notice.

kq.action: choose a record and show who receives a service window

Mark the schedule gaps and give Lin a way to hear the next reader.

missions.title: A Notice Within Reach
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How does a notice help someone find the line they actually need?

objectives.title: Give the rule, counts and next check more room on the notice.

missions.title: Three Loads, Four Marks
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When can a chance model guide a receiving plan, and where do arrivals need to be observed?

objectives.title: Load both sealed practice trays at dispatch.
Group the possible arrivals and check the crew’s release time.
Try a receiving arrangement and visit the installed practice setup.

missions.title: A Place Beyond the Steps
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When does an empty place count as access?
missions.stake: Ade has one ramp for the practice board. The North Steps and Canal Walk readers have different times to reach it.

objectives.title: Check the stair and ramp requests at both stops.
Open the same two trial queues with the ramp tile at each stop.
Post a practice queue and visit the stop that gets the ramp.

journal.text: Changing the recorded requests changed the route under the same rule. We kept the first window counts beside the rule and asked where and when readers can reach the stops.

In the equal, independent draw model, 40 of 64 ordered arrivals shared a mark. The fixed trays showed whether three known loads fit. The crew’s shared release time changed what it was reasonable to assume about actual arrival times.
The trial lanes had the same place count. An empty place could still be behind steps. One ramp changed who could come through, and the two crews still needed different times.

moments.did: You held one rule steady while trying the requests from two routes.
moments.prompt: Who could leave a request through one route and miss the other?

moments.did: You helped a reader ask for a place and time they could reach.
moments.prompt: Which part of a notice might look different to the next reader?

moments.did: You made room for someone to follow each reason and each figure.
moments.prompt: Where could someone go to check how a notice was made?

chronicle.title: Four windows on a notice
chronicle.text: The public board gives both district counts and the rule that shared the four library windows.

chronicle.title: Places and times still open
chronicle.text: A reader asked which window they could reach. The next request round will leave room for a time and a place.

hints.text: A new passage has opened in the Nexus.
Look for the Civic Machine sign near the archive crossings.
Step into the dispatch hall and find the trial console.
Keeper Ade stands by the console. The paths lead to the public desk and the canal.
Two crews collected requests in different places.
Find the public desk at North Steps and the walking board at Canal Walk.
Read both slips. See where the walking numbers differ and what happened to repeated requests.
Bring the desk slip and walking slip back to the dispatch hall before comparing the two tallies.
A draft heading calls one request route complete.
Try a rule using the desk tally at Ade’s console.
Choose the same rule again with the joined tally after reading both slips.
Check the draft desk heading against the extra requests on the walking slip. The checked heading appears after a matched trial.
Keep the joined tally while changing how windows are shared.
Find the three rule controls on the trial console.
Try a second distinct rule with the joined tally.
Check which districts receive windows under your two rules. Take those results to Lin.
The rule can be part of the notice readers see.
Visit Route Clerk Lin at the North Steps desk.
Choose a rule you tried on the joined tally.
Put the four windows on the notice and read the public result by the desk.
A reader tried to use the numbers on the first notice.
Follow the crossing to Canal Walk.
Find the reply on the canal rail after you publish.
Read what a person working late still needs to know about the windows.
The reply asks for a time and a place.
Bring the reader’s reply back to Lin.
Keep the trial counts dated and open a way to record times and reachable places.
Choose an evening request visit or a wider walking round. Then find the revised notice.
A reader at the bench needs room to trace the lines.
Visit Lin after posting the revised notice.
Ask for a wider notice with separate lines for the rule, counts and next check.
Look for the larger notice by the bench after you commission it.
Two sealed trays wait at Library Dispatch.
One tray is near the west passage. The other is near the cart beside the east passage.
Unclip the slips and place the three loads on each tray.
Use the red tray, then the blue tray. Compare loads waiting with empty marks.
Check the counting rack and find out when the couriers can leave work.
The four-mark rack is in Dispatch. The crew’s slip is at the Canal Walk bench.
Make the separate rows in the rack, then group the rows that share an arrival mark.
Fill both sets of rows at the rack. Read the end-of-shift slip at Canal Walk.
The practice dispatch board has room for one receiving arrangement.
Use the board near the east side of Library Dispatch.
A helper can take a second load at one mark. Separate reservations need times people can actually use.
Choose a setup. The helper goes to Canal Walk, or the staggered board goes to North Steps. Read the selected setup when you arrive.
The ramp board needs a slip from each stop.
Visit North Steps to the west and Canal Walk to the east from Dispatch.
Read the stair and ramp slip at each stop. The bell or shift tells you when people can reach it.
Take the North Steps slip off the west post and the Canal Walk slip by the approach boards. Bring both to Ade’s lane board.
Some people can use either lane. Some need the step-free approach.
There are two sockets and one ramp tile. Try both placements with the same request sets.
Place the ramp at North Steps and open both queues. Move the ramp to Canal Walk and open both queues again.
Compare the empty places with the people waiting after each placement. Plans with the same total can leave different people waiting.
The trial still owes the waiting readers a real place and time.
Choose a stop for the practice ramp.
Place the ramp at the chosen stop then use Post this practice queue.
Walk to the chosen stop. Read the ramp notice and see which readers still need a usable time.

sources.title: Separate Wea convention, 7 Stat. 116
sources.locator: October 26, 1809. Preamble and passage recording the Wea representatives’ declaration. NARA 94278486.
sources.supports: The convention separately lists William Henry Harrison and Wea representatives at Vincennes. The text records a declaration concerning the September agreement and its separate article.

sources.title: Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma: Constitution
sources.locator: Official public PDF, Article I on the name, Article VI on government, and the 1999 amendment certificate.
sources.supports: The constitutional copy names this government and describes its executive, legislative and judicial branches. Its closing material includes a 1999 amendment certificate.

cards.title: The separate Wea convention
cards.text: The 26 October 1809 agreement at Vincennes records a declaration by listed Wea representatives about the Fort Wayne treaty and a separate article. William Henry Harrison appears as the United States commissioner.
cards.limits: The record gives the named parties and terms of this agreement. Its words cannot establish how free the negotiations were, how every Wea person understood them, or what other nations agreed to.

cards.title: A constitutional record of a present-day government
cards.text: Article I of the public constitution names the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. Article VI describes an executive led by the Chief, a legislature made up of the Business Committee, and a judiciary.
cards.limits: This is the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma’s own constitutional record. The Absentee Shawnee Tribe and the Shawnee Tribe govern separately. The copy gives no account of political authority in 1809.

exhibits.name: Vincennes convention with Wea representatives
exhibits.dateKind: Date the convention gives for the agreement. Its ratification and proclamation occurred in January 1810.
exhibits.summary: This separate record names Wea representatives and gives their recorded declaration about the September agreement. Article 5 of the earlier treaty directs the reader to a separate record.
exhibits.altText: Original illustration of a paper folio with two marked edges.

exhibits.name: Constitution of the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma
exhibits.dateText: Public copy with a certified 1999 amendment
exhibits.dateKind: The year belongs to the amendment certification included with the copy. The preamble asserts the Tribe’s inherent sovereignty.
exhibits.summary: The Tribe publishes its own constitutional copy. Article I gives its full name. Article VI describes the branches of its government.
exhibits.altText: Original illustration of a paper folio with two marked edges.
